newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu under pressure to sack minister.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu under pressure to sack minister.

text.p: Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu came under pressure on Wednesday to sack his justice minister over a corruption scandal that will not die.

Netanyahu's government survived intact when, for lack of evidence, both he and Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi escaped prosecutors' indictment on Sunday in the short-lived appointment last January of an attorney-general.
But prosecutors cited "real suspicions" about their roles in the affair, prompting demands for action against Hanegbi from some within the government and Netanyahu's Likud party.
"I have no intention of abandoning my post," Hanegbi told Israel Radio. Netanyahu's office refused comment.
Palestinians demanded that Netanyahu refocus attention on Middle East peacemaking, still in crisis since he started work on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem last month.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah said on Wednesday that U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright had called Arafat overnight.
"It was agreed to continue contacts to reach suggestions that will solve the current crisis," Abu Rdainah told Reuters.

Israeli legislator Binyamin Begin, son of Likud founder Menachem Begin, and Industry and Trade Minister Natan Sharansky, Netanyahu's confidant, both demanded that Hanegbi -- as the country's overseer of justice -- be forced to resign.
"Mr Hanegbi, according to my best judgment, cannot continue in his post of justice minister," Begin told Israel Radio.
Begin resigned as science minister in Netanyahu's government over Israel's handing over most of the West Bank town of Hebron to Palestinian rule in January. He staunchly opposes Netanyahu.
Sharansky said his Yisrael ba-Aliya party wanted Hanegbi out. He said Netanyahu had promised unspecified "changes" after the Jewish Passover holiday ending on Monday.
Otherwise, Sharansky said, he would take his party's seven seats out of the coalition, denying Netanyahu his 66-54 parliamentary majority.
"If there are no changes we will not stay," he said.
Hanegbi, a 40-year-old lawyer, has impeccable right-wing credentials. His mother Geula Cohen was a leading member of the now defunct ultra-nationalist Tehiya party.
Yet even former Likud prime minister Yitzhak Shamir has criticised his abilities, telling the newspaper Maariv in February that Hanegbi would be unfit "even after 50 years on the job".

The calls for Hanegbi to leave, along with demands for a state inquiry and High Court challenges this week to the prosecutors' report, ensure the scandal will dog Netanyahu for some time despite his having said the issue was behind him.

Neither he nor the High Court was expected to make any decisions before the end of the week-long Jewish Passover holiday next Monday night. Legal experts said chances were slim the court would force prosecutors to press charges.
The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, open for the first time since the prosecutors' report, began the day slightly up.
"The effects of this affair on the financial market in Israel are over for the time being," Eli Nahum, of Zannex Securities, told Reuters.
Prosecutors said only Netanyahu's political ally Aryeh Deri, on trial in another matter, should be indicted while Netanyahu's director-general Avigdor Lieberman, should face further investigation.

A Channel One television report spurred the police inquiry into the appointment of Likud activist and lawyer Roni Bar-On in January. It alleged Deri coerced Netanyahu into appointing Bar-On, who would offer him a plea bargain.
Bar-On quit 12 hours after taking office amid a public outcry that he was a legal lightweight unqualified for the job.
